The theoretical framework of phonons in crystals with broken time and space symmetry has been successfully developed. Our analysis shows that the phonon Hall effect arises from topological features in the crystal's wave vector space. We discovered that the phonon Hall effect is not exclusive to dielectric materials, but is also a distinct phenomenon in metallic crystals. Furthermore, our findings indicate that in metallic crystals, the phonon Hall conductivity is influenced by both the wave vector polarization and inversion of charge transport between opposite bands.

A new, wide-field imaging technique, known as Wide Field Shifted Excitation Raman Difference Spectroscopy, has been developed. This technique employs a Nod and Shuffle Technical Interface on a Raman microscope and acquires up to 256 spectra at random points on a 1mm^2 area within 2 minutes. The proposed method has two variations: Wide Field Shifted Excitation Raman Spectroscopy and Wide Field Shifted Raman Spectroscopy. These techniques can be used for chemical imaging and can be applied to complex biological samples. The proposed algorithm has been tested on various RSCM-based spectral imaging techniques and demonstrates significant improvements in signal-to-background ratios, processing times and spectral resolution. The algorithm's effectiveness has been demonstrated using RSCM on Raman and fluorescence images of a single cell and Raman images of a plant leaf. The proposed algorithm has also been tested on RSCM on Raman and fluorescence images of a single cell and RSCM on Raman images of a plant leaf.

This article provides matrix extensions of the Fejér and Levin-Stečkin inequalities. Furthermore, it develops a matrix inequality for the circulant block Toeplitz operator and applies this to derive lower bounds on the eigenvalues of the circulant block Toeplitz matrix.

We examine the average null energy condition at the horizon of an evaporating black hole in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence. By calculating the quantum corrections to the stress-energy tensor, we find that they cause the condition to be satisfied. However, a notable finding is that this satisfaction comes with a cost, ultimately leading the black hole to evaporate. Notably, our results differ from a previous study and contradict a claimed result. To resolve this discrepancy, we point out a critical oversight and emphasize the importance of accurately translating the geometry between the bulk and boundary perspectives.

This collection of course notes focuses on breaking down the intricate structure of Conformal Field Theory (CFT) into manageable components, with an emphasis on S-matrix, crossing symmetry, and the entanglement entropy. It begins with an examination of CFT basics, followed by a detailed exploration of the S-matrix and its applications. Next, the entanglement entropy in CFT is thoroughly explored, culminating in an in-depth discussion of the two-dimensional case, which includes a thorough analysis of the Ellis Wysocki state and its connections. Furthermore, an introduction to four-dimensional CFT is provided, with a specific focus on the unitarity constraints of the four-point functions. Additionally, a chapter is dedicated to the modular Hamiltonian and its connections to the stress-energy tensor two-point function.

This article introduces the Industrial Control System Cybersecurity Testbed MLM, a hierarchical model that assesses the effectiveness of testbeds in ICS cybersecurity research and development. The ICS-CTM2 model provides a framework that aligns with existing research, highlights current testbed shortcomings, and proposes future research directions to create comprehensive ICS cybersecurity testbeds.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, the primary issue arises from agents encountering non-stationarity during cooperative tasks. The previous approach to address this problem was by assuming a single reward and having agents learn independently, but we've developed an alternative solution by utilizing a representation of each agent's overall value, enabling them to adjust their actions accordingly. This new method, based on a greedy algorithm, enables agents to adjust their behavior in response to the changing environment, but through our experiments, we've found that combining this approach with others yields the best results when used alongside the previous method.

Pretrained language models have become the foundation for various NLP applications, but research has uncovered biases that can be inherited by downstream models, compromising their objectivity. However, existing bias detection methods often rely on general-purpose bias indicators that can lead to false positives, especially for biases like stereotypical bias. To address this issue, we developed a novel framework for detecting stereotypical bias that is grounded in theories from social psychology and is specifically designed to avoid false positives. We evaluated our framework on the StereoSet, a newly created dataset of 1,500 stereotypical statements from six domains, and found that our domain-specific features outperformed general-purpose features in detecting stereotypical bias. Furthermore, our study demonstrated that removing these biases from pre-trained language models can significantly reduce their influence in downstream tasks. The StereoSet dataset is available for public use at https://stereset.org

In cellular networks, remote electrical tilt plays a crucial role in optimizing base station tilt settings, and our research has successfully applied off-policy reinforcement learning to tackle this challenge. A remote electrical tilt setting can be viewed as a type of observation adjustment that enhances channel quality, and our approach uses a model-free deep reinforcement learning method to determine the optimal setting for these adjustments. We have developed a novel off-policy deep reinforcement learning algorithm, which uses deep neural networks to establish an optimal adjustment policy, and our results show that this algorithm outperforms conventional methods in real-world scenarios. Moreover, our approach allows cellular network operators to easily integrate the learned policy into their existing systems, thereby improving their performance.

A multi-measurement approach to determine the CKM angle gamma has been developed by combining the results of three LHCb experiments. This method enables the direct exclusion of values for gamma that conflict with the results obtained from each individual analysis. By incorporating all available data from LHCb to date, the analysis provides a measurement of gamma that offers improved precision over previously published outcomes from individual experiments.

Several properties of complex ellipsoids among convex bodies in n-dimensional space have been rigorously established in relation to their sections and projections, a crucial concept for further research. Establishing criteria for complex symmetry within this framework provides a valuable approach.

The collection, trading, and sharing of personal data are at the center of high-stakes legal, ethical, and scientific debates. Yet, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding the attitudes of everyday people towards the buying, selling, and sharing of personal data. To address this gap, we conducted a study consisting of focus groups and surveys with 76 non-experts, exploring their perceptions of the ethical implications of data markets. Our research reveals that laypeople tend to prioritize control over their data, rather than the potential financial gains. Additionally, it becomes evident that people are willing to consider utility as a motivating factor when engaging in the trade of personal data, but only when they feel they have control over these transactions.

A novel approach to detect FTN signaling called List Deep-Sphere Decoding (L-SD) has been developed, which offers improved performance over traditional soft decision decoding methods. L-SD employs a deep neural network to classify symbols from a broader list of candidates, thereby mitigating the computational complexity that arises from the iterative process of soft decision decoding. In contrast to other deep learning-based decoders, L-SD is grounded in the theoretical framework of list sphere decoding and can leverage the benefits of non-linear minimum mean square error channel estimation. Furthermore, a training method for the deep neural network has been established, which relies on simulated FTN channel symbols and can adapt to varying FTN symbol spacings without the need for retraining. Simulation results confirm that the proposed L-SD outperforms traditional soft decision decoding and supports the theoretical findings.

This study introduces order topology and Frink ideal topology to effect algebras. It then examines the topological characteristics of these spaces, including their compactness, Hausdorff property, separation, and Borel spaces. The investigation also explores the connections between these spaces and their respective Borel spaces. In particular, certain implications related to the order topology and Frink ideal topology within both self-adjoint effect algebras and probability algebras are examined.

Recent advancements in deep learning models have achieved exceptional performance in image classification tasks. Nevertheless, these models often rely heavily on the presence of specific patterns in the training data, leading to overfitting issues. To mitigate this problem, data augmentation techniques have been widely applied, but they typically introduce random transformations to images without considering their inherent structure. To address this limitation, we propose SaliencyMix, a novel data augmentation approach that selectively hides specific regions of an image based on the model's learned focus points. By leveraging saliency maps and image segmentation, SaliencyMix applies pixel-level transformations to guide image generation, effectively preserving the core features necessary for recognition. Through this process, SaliencyMix helps to reduce the reliance on edge data and promote the model to extract more fundamental characteristics from the training images. To evaluate the effectiveness of SaliencyMix, we conducted experiments on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, and the results demonstrate that this approach yields better generalization and a more stable learning process.

We focus on the infinite-dimensional rational Iwahori--Hecke algebra $H_\infty(S)$, which is related to a finite reflection group $S$ acting on a vector space. Our research reveals that non-degenerate, $\mathbb{Z}$-bilinear forms on $H_\infty(S)$ yield right modules over the corresponding affine Demazure algebra, demonstrating a categorification of the symmetric functions in finite rank. Furthermore, we examine the properties of non-degenerate bilinear forms on $H_\infty(S)$ and show that they lead to isometric representations of the group $S$ on a Hilbert space, thus generalizing a well-known result for finite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebras.

A new cosmic shear correlation function is introduced, sensitive to galaxy orientation, which is directly related to the Guckenberg tensor in Horndeski gravity theory.  The Guckenberg tensor describes how light interacts with matter in a way dependent on time, location, and orientation.  The correlation function's sensitivity to the Guckenberg tensor is proportional to the product of two galaxy orientation vectors, making it a good indicator of galaxy alignment.  The correlation function can be used to test modified gravity theories by analyzing cosmic shear data, as it directly relates to the Guckenberg tensor.  The signal strength depends on the strength of the modified gravity effect and the accuracy of galaxy orientation data, with current surveys such as LSST and Euclid potentially providing sufficient information to detect the signal.

In this research, we explore the intricate relationships between deformation, elasticity, and the non-conventional viscoelastic behavior exhibited by discrete collections of deformable particles. Through the application of the Network Monte Carlo simulation method, we investigate the dynamic properties of two-dimensional arrays of cylindrical particles that interact via deformable, flexible connections. Our study reveals novel insights into the system's viscoelastic behavior, shedding light on the fundamental principles governing the intricate interplay between deformation processes and stress accumulation within these structured networks. The outcomes of our simulation hold significance for understanding the viscoelastic properties of a diverse array of biological and synthetic materials, such as protein-based networks, polymers in solution, hydrogels, and composite materials.

A computational study is presented, utilizing the G4 Generalized-Atom and G4 Brenner Embedded-Atom-Model potentials to investigate the melting behavior of gold nanoparticles with sizes ranging from 1 nm to 10 nm. Through classical molecular dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that these potentials effectively capture the structural and thermodynamic properties of these nanoparticles, including the phase transition from the solid to liquid state. Additionally, we employ a novel, data-driven approach to identify the phase transition, which relies solely on the particle's mean squared displacement and temperature. This method is particularly valuable for analyzing the melting process in nanoparticles that exhibits distinct characteristics at the intermediate temperature range, differing from bulk gold's superheated liquid state.

This is the beginning of a series focused on the generalizations and uses of well-known theorems within variational bifurcation theory. Leveraging parameterized versions of splitting theorems in Morse theory, some prominent bifurcation theorems are broadened for potential operators by relaxing conventional requirements for the differentiability of associated functionals and the invertibility of their second derivatives.

We examine flavor models incorporating a $Z_N$ symmetry, with $N$ flavors of each type, subject to specific constraints, resulting in a balance between up and down quark masses. This model is capable of explaining a wide range of mass ratios for quarks and charged leptons, including their first and second generation, third generation, and the ratio of muon to tau decay widths.
We derive alternative representations of (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials using the fermionic p-adic q-integral on Zp, in conjunction with weighted q-Bernstein polynomials.

Real-world healthcare decision-making often involves complex, long-term sequences of treatments, making it difficult to accurately assess the long-term effects of those treatments using traditional methods. To address this challenge, we've developed a new approach that utilizes reinforcement learning to estimate long-term treatment outcomes in such scenarios. By framing the problem as a Markov decision process, we've created a method that accounts for the dynamic nature of the sequences and their influence on subsequent treatment choices. Our approach enables the estimation of the value function, which provides a comprehensive assessment of the long-term effects of a given treatment choice. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through an analysis of a large electronic health record dataset and compare it to a more traditional method. The results reveal that our approach not only offers a more accurate estimate of the long-term effects but also provides a more detailed understanding of the dynamic relationships between treatments over time.

To address the limitations of case-control studies in inferring cause-and-effect relationships, researchers often employ case-control studies even when recall bias is suspected. A common strategy is to control for the bias using survey data from a cohort, but this approach is problematic. When recall bias affects the cases, it leads to biased estimates of the causal effect, and controlling for the bias using cohort data is not possible. Furthermore, even when recall bias is absent, using cohort data to control for confounding results in biased case estimates, and controlling for the bias using conditional control variables does not restore consistency. As a result, current methods are ineffective in addressing the bias. A novel framework is proposed, grounded in causal inference, to address these issues. The new framework is based on the concept of structural equations and offers a new perspective on the problems associated with case-control studies. A novel estimator is developed, which is shown to be unbiased under certain conditions. The estimator is grounded in causal inference and is shown to be robust to the recall bias model. A simulation study demonstrates the effectiveness of the new estimator. The proposed framework is applied to a study examining the relationship between early-life socioeconomic status and adult labor market outcomes in the US, and the results reveal a significant socioeconomic effect on college completion.

Generative models can be learned efficiently using maximum likelihood training, but existing methods that utilize invertible layers face a major limitation - they require models with unbounded complexity, specifically $O(n^2)$, to accurately represent data distributions. This constraint is circumvented by implementing a more intricate layer structure, thereby validating the theoretical framework that underpins invertible layers for maximum likelihood training. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the optimal model for this specific task involves incorporating an unbounded number of invertible layers. Interestingly, our experiments demonstrate that models with $O(n)$ complexity can still effectively capture data distributions. We also examine the implications of this discovery and its potential extensions to more complex scenarios, such as multimodal data sets.

The Smart City initiative leverages data-driven decision making, but
understanding the complex relationships within vast amounts of data remains
a significant challenge. To address this, we propose an innovative approach
that integrates attribute correlation analysis with smart city data to facilitate
informed decision making. Our method involves three core components: (1)
a data transformation technique that preserves key correlations; (2) a
visualization tool that enables users to interactively explore the
underlying patterns; and (3) a set of automated features to aid user
discovery. Case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in
uncovering significant trends, pinpointing anomalies, and simplifying
complex data, ultimately leading to more data-savvy decisions.

This paper explores the development of efficient numerical methods to solve two types of problems: a reaction-diffusion equation and the generalized Stokes equations, using the HDG-P0 scheme. We examine the algebraic properties of the resulting matrices and propose an optimization strategy for choosing the degrees of freedom in the boundary for better numerical performance. We also introduce an optimized multigrid preconditioner that achieves superior convergence rates compared to traditional methods. Numerical results confirm our theoretical findings and demonstrate the benefits of our approach.

A new sensitivity analysis is proposed to assess the impact of missing data on causal findings. This analysis is based on the E-value, which estimates the proportion of causes that wouldn't be detected even with optimal observation. Due to the intractability of the E-value posterior distribution, a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm is developed to approximate it. This algorithm is then applied to a real-world dataset from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis to determine how smoking and pack-years affect cardiovascular disease risk factors.

In crossover trials with missing gene expression data, a multivariate mixed-effects model is employed to analyze the data by both complete case and full data methods. The complete case method disregards the information from missing gene expressions, whereas the full data method utilizes an EM algorithm to derive a likelihood-based estimator. Although the complete case method yields consistent estimators, the likelihood-based estimator is generally more precise. To compare the performance of both methods, a simulation study and real-world data analysis were conducted. The simulation study demonstrated that the likelihood-based estimator tends to produce smaller standard errors than the complete case method when the data follow a normal distribution. However, when gene expressions were skewed, the complete case method sometimes outperformed the full data method. The real-world data analysis, focusing on a specific dataset, revealed that LILP, a likelihood-based estimator, provided a more precise and efficient analysis compared to FC and CC methods.

This study introduces the concept of a weakly monoidal category, which is a category with a biproduct structure that satisfies certain modified associativity and commutativity properties. The construction of this category involves building on cohomology and homotopy theories of specific types of algebras. Notably, it provides an alternative representation for the Stasheff A(n)-space, specifically its topological characteristics. Furthermore, it connects the A(n) spaces to a sequence of geometrically-defined associahedra, which are linked to a category of graded algebras and have implications for the study of their deformation theory.

Memory-centric computing relies heavily on DRAM as a primary memory and storage medium, yet its functionality is largely defined by the constraints of the DRAM standard. To address this limitation, we propose the development of custom in-DRAM functionalities that can be tailored to specific computing needs, enhancing the efficiency of memory-intensive applications. However, creating such custom functionalities poses significant challenges, particularly the need for extensive testing to ensure their reliability, which is both costly and time-consuming. To overcome this obstacle, we introduce CODIC, an innovative, low-cost platform for enabling custom in-DRAM functionalities. CODIC leverages a hardware-software framework that facilitates the integration of user-defined logic into DRAM chips, enabling the development of custom memory-related functionalities such as data compression, data re-routing, and data preprocessing. Additionally, CODIC's built-in hardware accelerates the execution of testbench programs, significantly reducing the time required for testing and ensuring the reliability of the custom functionalities. To demonstrate the capabilities of CODIC, we have developed and tested several functional modules, including a data compression module that achieves a 1.7x improvement in bandwidth, 40% reduction in energy consumption, and 1.2x decrease in DRAM die area compared to standard DRAM chips.

Network management and orchestration involve a complex interplay between network complexity, the quantity of managed elements, and the intricacy of their interactions. This necessitates a comprehensive approach to management and orchestration that accounts for the dynamic nature of networks. By integrating the principles of virtualization, networks can now accommodate diverse, dynamic, and stateful applications, which demand sophisticated management capabilities. This can be achieved through a paradigm shift towards a more decentralized, user-centric, and context-aware network that incorporates data-driven decision making and automated processes. To address the challenges arising from this new paradigm, functional programming offers a unique solution that can provide a structured approach to managing network resources, including virtualized network functions, network orchestration, and other network components. This paper aims to explore the potential of functional programming in designing network management solutions by examining its application in a real-world context.

This study investigates the efficiency of quantum gates in the context of encoded quantum information. We examine the impact of stabilizer gates on the error correction process and propose a cost function to assess their performance. Our analysis focuses on the most commonly used gates in the circuit model, revealing that two-body and multi-body interactions have distinct effects on the stability of encoded qubits. We discovered that, in the toric code, single-body gates are not optimal and that including multi-body interactions can lead to improved gate performance. Our findings also suggest that incorporating multiple-body interactions can result in lower energy consumption and reduced gate costs.

The OPUS system streamlines access to analysis and simulation tools by providing a unified interface. Implementing the IVOA-defined Universal Worker System pattern, it offers REST-based job control for efficient asynchronous execution on work clusters. Additionally, OPUS incorporates the IVOA Provenance Data Model to track job provenance and results. With standardized APIs, the component-based architecture facilitates seamless integration and expansion, enabling the addition of new tools and functionalities.

Digital game-based learning has become a prominent approach in contemporary education. The potential benefits include enhanced student engagement, satisfaction, and performance. However, research has primarily focused on undergraduate and master's levels, leaving a gap in education at the school and high school levels. The proposed research aims to create and integrate interactive elements into courses for designing and managing complex wireless networks. The primary objectives are to develop a comprehensive educational approach, create and implement digital games for real-world applications, and evaluate the effectiveness of this novel pedagogy. The expected outcomes include (i) a practical methodology for incorporating interactivity into network science education, (ii) three digital games that simulate real-world scenarios, and (iii) a thorough assessment of this approach. The proposed research will focus on network science and its applications in wireless networks, leveraging the IEEE 802.11 standard. The initial phase will involve designing and developing three digital games that cater to different learning styles and will be implemented in a classroom setting. The subsequent phase will involve assessing student performance, engagement, and understanding of project-based and game-based learning methods.

The combination of ozone and molecular oxygen is a reliable indicator of past photochemistry in atmospheres, particularly in rocks and minerals. This method relies on the balance between oxygen and ozone, which is often assumed constant. This assumption holds true in atmospheres dominated by oxygen and non-reactive gases like N2, CO2, and CH4, as well as in those containing no oxygen. However, atmospheres rich in oxygen and halogen-containing gases disrupt this balance, leading to an overestimation of past oxygen levels when relying solely on the O3-O2 relationship. This issue is more pronounced in atmospheres with an O3 to O2 ratio of 0.1 and higher, rather than those at O3 to O2 equilibrium, and becomes increasingly significant in atmospheres containing halogen gases at concentrations of 0.01%, particularly when considering the O3 to O2 ratio is above 0.5. This method's limitations highlight its unsuitability for atmospheres rich in oxygen and suggest alternative approaches for estimating past atmospheric composition.

The quantum Hall effect's robustness under various perturbations has been extensively researched, particularly in two-dimensional systems. However, the presence of three dimensions introduces novel dynamics, such as band crossings and level repulsions, which significantly impact the stability of the quantum Hall effect. By employing numerical simulations, we investigate the impact of these dimensions on quantum Hall states in a three-dimensional Hofstadter model. Our research reveals that nonequilibrium surface currents in these states are highly resilient to external perturbations, including magnetic field fluctuations and boundary deformations, due to their quantized nature. Moreover, we find that these currents are resistant to interactions with level crossings and even level repulsions, as long as the magnetic flux remains finite. Our results have implications for the development of quantum Hall devices in three-dimensional systems, as they suggest that the stability of equilibrium and nonequilibrium currents can be maintained even in the presence of imperfections.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation (NMT) have led to significant performance improvements. However, NMT models trained on multiple languages often struggle to translate certain domain-specific terms accurately, as they rely on general knowledge from the training data. To address this issue, we explore the effectiveness of domain-specific adaptations for NMT models, utilizing a dataset of English and Russian radiological reports with corresponding translations in six additional languages. By fine-tuning a pre-trained mNMT model on a small Russian radiology corpus and evaluating its performance on both general and specialized texts, we found that the model's performance in specialized text scenarios improves substantially after fine-tuning. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of fine-tuning on translation accuracy in specific areas like radiology terminology and abbreviations, which we extracted and annotated from the dataset for a more detailed analysis.

A system consisting of non-thermal electrons, warm ions, and positively charged stationary dust is used to investigate modified-ion-acoustic waves. The influence of positively charged stationary dust on the properties of such waves is examined, with a particular focus on its effect on the formation of solitary and shock waves. The results indicate that the dust particles have a substantial impact on the waves' properties. The wave speed is found to increase with the density ratio but decrease with the ion temperature. The dust particles' influence leads to a reduction in wave speed and a rise in ion acoustic speed. The wave speed is also found to be higher in cases with lower ion fluid temperatures and higher dust concentrations. The dust particles have a substantial impact on wave speed and soliton properties, which increases with the ion fluid temperature. The shock wave properties, including peak density and electric field, increase with the dust concentration and ion fluid temperature. The wave properties, including ion acoustic speed and wave speed, increase with the dust concentration and ion fluid temperature. The wave properties, including soliton width and amplitude, increase with the ion fluid temperature. The ion fluid temperature has a substantial impact on wave properties, which is in agreement with previous studies.

Recent research has shown that multilingual models can significantly enhance information retrieval across various languages. However, training such models on extensive text data can be extremely resource-intensive. This paper presents an efficient approach to develop a multilingual model for dense retrieval using an unsupervised strategy. This involves training the model on English data and applying orthographic transformations to generate representations for other languages, without requiring parallel data for each language. Our proposed method includes a novel unsupervised loss function that incorporates contextual information for generating sentence representations. This approach outperforms a baseline model in 9 languages, achieving improved performance in 7 languages according to the Hits@1 metric.

Multimodal learning, which combines information from various data types, is a crucial area of research. However, the development of universal multimodal models has been hindered by the challenge of balancing the representation of different modalities. This paper presents a novel method, Prototypical Modal Rebalance (PMR), designed to mitigate the imbalances that occur during pre-training of multimodal models. By using a contrastive learning framework, the new method encourages the different components of a multimodal representation to become increasingly distinct. This process is facilitated by the use of a set of unique reference points that are shared across different modalities. This shared representation enables the development of more nuanced and balanced multimodal connections. Moreover, the new method allows for the integration of information from multiple sources, including not just the initial multimodal representation but also the intermediate layers of a neural network. This allows the different components of a model to adapt to each other more effectively. The results of experiments on a range of visual and language-based tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the new method, which outperforms existing approaches to multimodal learning.

Using the Wigner function formalism, the relativistic Boltzmann equation for particles interacting via vector forces is developed in terms of moments. The equation's collision term is expressed as a form of anisotropic scattering with a specified $2\to 2$ cross-section. The angular dependence of the scattering amplitude is represented by a series expansion in terms of Legendre polynomials up to the fourth order. The relativistic transport model, derived from this equation, is applied to study properties of hot dense nuclear matter. The model is used to calculate various physical observables such as pressure, energy density, speed of sound, and ratio of these values. The results of this relativistic model are compared to those obtained from a non-relativistic $2\to 2$ scattering model.

This study explores the application of tensor-train networks in improving the performance of ASR systems. A novel approach was developed to apply data augmentation techniques to tensor-train networks, utilizing acoustic features as input. The method was evaluated on the Librispeech dataset and found to achieve comparable results to traditional CNNs and antrietors, while requiring significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, the augmented tensor-train model was found to outperform other models in certain settings. The ability of the model to capture local patterns in speech by its network structure was identified as the key factor contributing to its success.

The simulation of open quantum systems is significantly accelerated through the application of quantum dynamical backaction, which can be effectively harnessed via the quantum-jump method. This method relies on the continuous monitoring of a non-Hermitian extension of the system's Hamiltonian, typically derived from a specific representation of the master equation. We demonstrate that distinct master equation representations, including those utilizing the diagonal or off-diagonal Hermitian part, or the Liouvillian and diagonal off-diagonal degenerate forms, yield equivalent quantum-jump evolutions. This equivalence allows for the application of any representation, as long as the evolution is well defined. We then derive the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and jump operators for each representation and verify the equivalence of the corresponding Fokker-Planck equations. We also derive the jump operators for an arbitrary master equation form and establish a general quantum dynamical backaction criterion. This is followed by the derivation of the equivalent non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and jump operators for a class of master equations that incorporate arbitrary initial system states.

This study explores the influence of plasmonic aluminum nanostructures on silicon thin-film solar cells, with a focus on end-toched devices. We examine the effects of using different aluminum nanostructure shapes, including spheres, ellipsoids, and pyramids, on enhanced light absorption. Our findings indicate that aluminum nanostructures with a pyramidal shape yield the highest optical absorption enhancement for thin-film solar cells, surpassing those with spherical or elliptical shapes. Furthermore, we examine the optical absorption enhancement for different solar cell thicknesses and identify a common pattern in the optimal pyramidal shape enhancement. We also compare the optical absorption enhancement to previously reported results for thicker thin-film solar cells, revealing that the pyramidal shape factor plays a crucial role in the optimal absorption location. Our results have significant implications for improving end-cut solar cell performance.

The concept of data reducibility plays a significant role in the study of problems solvable in polynomial time (PTIME). It enables the creation of a hierarchy of problems, with each issue in this hierarchy being reducible to the next one. By examining the data reducibility of problems to each other, researchers can determine the relative difficulty of various problems. Notably, the current understanding of problems solvable in polynomial time (PTIME) is limited to those that can be solved using a counting approach, with no known problems that require a more complex reduction. By introducing a new type of reduction, with restrictions on counting, we have identified a subset of problems in PTIME that can be solved without relying on counting. It is hypothesized that this reduction captures a significant portion of problems in PTIME that can be solved without counting, providing new insights into the nature of problems in this category.

Deep learning models, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have achieved top performance in various video recognition tasks. However, their high complexity hinders real-time video processing due to lengthy training times and large power consumption. To address this issue, we developed a novel co-design framework that optimizes LSTM network training and prediction while minimizing hardware resource utilization. Our framework utilizes tensor decomposition to compress model weights and reduces memory requirements, enabling parallelism on multiple processors. Additionally, we designed an energy-efficient LSTM training algorithm utilizing quantization and data sparsification to accelerate video training without sacrificing accuracy. The proposed framework was integrated into an FPGA-based system, providing a complete co-design solution that accelerates both LSTM training and prediction.

This study examines MAVLink security vulnerabilities and outlines a secure framework utilizing TLS/SSL encryption to safeguard MAVLink traffic. Given the protocol's widespread use among unmanned systems, researchers have previously explored simulating attacks on drones but have neglected to investigate actual exploitation scenarios. Our investigation into real-world deployments of the MAVLink protocol reveals numerous security risks inherent to its design and implementation. We identify potential risks associated with the protocol's implementation in Ardupilot/PX4 based systems through various attack vectors. To address these vulnerabilities, we develop a secure solution utilizing TLS/SSL encryption, which we demonstrate can effectively prevent unauthorized access to these systems. We further emphasize the importance of secure protocol usage and suggest future enhancements to the MAVLink protocol to mitigate similar risks in future releases.

Emulating complex topologies on smaller, simpler setups is beneficial for training complex network algorithms, conducting network security tests, and designing network architectures. Kollaps is a software platform that enables users to create customizable, decentralized networks with dynamic complex topologies for various purposes. It features a dynamic, node-centric approach that allows for efficient, scalable networks with reduced costs. Kollaps includes a centralized management system, decentralized node management, and various tools for simulating real-world network behaviors. With Kollaps, users can establish and study diverse network topologies, including clusters, grids, hybrid networks, and customized configurations. This platform facilitates research and development in decentralized systems, network resilience, and distributed systems at large scales.

We previously introduced a unique mapping between specific solutions of Einstein's theory and a particular set of Maxwell's equations that share certain symmetry properties. This mapping can be interpreted in a unique way when considering a specific type of space that combines geometric and complex concepts. In this work, we further explore the underlying structure of this mapping by translating it into a specific mathematical problem involving null geodesics on that space. We also show that solutions with a type of rotation have a corresponding visual representation in the complex plane.

The Muon Tomography method leverages cosmic rays to create detailed 3D images of large underground spaces by using muons as probes, and advanced reconstruction algorithms to generate detailed maps. This technique holds significant potential for underground research facilities like the DUNE experiment. A working Muon Detector for Underground Tomography has been developed and tested, and its performance is evaluated using real data and simulated data, showcasing its potential in generating high-quality images of large caverns with high spatial resolution.

This study introduces an updated GLL parsing method capable of parsing not only context-free grammars but also parsing expression grammars with added support for lookahead. By integrating lookahead, this revised parsing method expands its capabilities. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed parsing algorithm is conducted, accompanied by a demonstration of a working implementation in a sample context.

This study explores the emission of vacuum Cherenkov radiation in a $Q$-theory environment where a charged particle's constant mass is replaced by temperature-dependent inertia. For the electromagnetic theory, we derive an analytical expression for the Cherenkov radiation wavelength. Furthermore, we examine how temperature affects the vacuum fine structure constant and the efficiency of Cherenkov radiation within the $Q$-theory framework. Our findings also include numerical examples of Cherenkov radiation spectra for both the electromagnetic and $Q$-theory environments.

Neural networks have excelled in various language tasks, yet their predictive abilities within language remain largely unexplored due to a lack of available data. To address this issue, we created a large-scale, multi-lingual dataset based on extensive annotated corpora of over 10 million tokens. This novel resource enables researchers to examine and compare how accurately neural models predict linguistic structures under different conditions, offering a benchmark for future studies. Our analysis indicates that the predictions made by neural models align with those of humans, while also revealing that the human brain processes predicted and non-predicted words differently, particularly when accounting for grammatical accuracy.

Our approach to learning the three-dimensional representation of objects from visual data involves a novel dataset of objects viewed from different angles as they spin in front of a camera. In contrast to traditional methods, we show that observing objects change pose provides significant insights for pose prediction. In fact, when compared to conventional image-based learning methods, our technique achieves near-optimal performance when the objects in question are viewed from a fixed pose. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our system excels at identifying an object's identity, given just a three-dimensional perspective, a capability that conventional methods often struggle with.

A quantum dot connected to superconducting leads through elastic co-tunneling enables the manipulation of Andreev bound states. By adjusting the size of the dot, these states can be created or destroyed. Additionally, by introducing phase differences between superconducting leads, the flow of current between the leads is controlled, producing a unique phenomenon known as crossed Andreev reflection. This phenomenon is typically short-lived as the dot's energy levels become broadened due to higher-order processes. However, in this study, we explore an alternative scenario where the dot's size is comparable to the superconducting gap. In this regime, the lifetime of the Andreev bound states is significantly extended, persisting over a broad energy range. Moreover, the system's ability to control the flow of current between the leads is further amplified, paving the way for potential applications in quantum information processing.

The transport of energetic particles in various astrophysical contexts is thought to be facilitated by magnetic reconnection. However, the mechanism behind their acceleration is still not fully understood. This study examines the effects of pitch-angle scattering on the particles within a magnetic reconnection setup. The research reveals that when particles are scattered in one direction, their distribution becomes asymmetrical, resulting in accelerated particles forming near the reconnection site. The transport of these accelerated particles to the surrounding area is hindered by the lack of sufficient scattering in the perpendicular direction. This asymmetrical distribution is observed in two different magnetic reconnection scenarios, specifically in the out-of-ejecta regime and when the reconnection is accompanied by inflow. The study's findings are relevant to the acceleration of particles in various astrophysical contexts, including solar flares and gamma-ray bursts.

We investigate the possibility of discovering new, elusive particles within the framework of electron-positron colliders, specifically focusing on the production of a $Z$ boson in conjunction with a Higgs boson. This research is conducted across the full available energy spectrum, taking into account the impact of various exotic states. We examine the sensitivity of this approach to specific models featuring light, lightweight scalars, scalar photons, and fermionic scalars, as well as the potential for two-body decays of the Higgs boson into pairs of exotic scalars. Our analysis reveals that the search for $e^+e^-\to Zh$ offers a more effective method for detecting exotic states with masses below 10 GeV, while Higgs diphoton decays are more suitable for identifying masses above 10 GeV.

A formula for the subdifferential of the joint numerical radius is formulated and subsequently utilized to establish constraints on the set of self-adjoint operators within a complex three-dimensional space.

The widespread adoption of the Internet has led to a significant increase in the collection of personal data from individuals, leading to concerns over data protection. As a result, privacy protection has become an essential issue, prompting the development of data anonymization techniques to safeguard user data. However, existing solutions have been insufficient in addressing the privacy needs of modern applications. A new paradigm, known as Differential Privacy, has emerged as a potential solution to ensure data privacy. Despite its growing potential, further research is required to fully integrate this technology into the financial sector. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the integration of financial data with Differential Privacy mechanisms, examining the feasibility of its applications and proposing a new framework for secure data sharing.

This research paper examines multifunctions with randomly selected outcomes, mapping subsets of a metric space to another metric space, focusing on the properties associated with their graph, or correlation, in relation to subgradients and convex analysis. A specific type of subgradient, called corugate, is introduced and studied in this context. We establish that the graph of regular corugates at the support of these mappings constitutes an orthogonal regular increasing set function, which in turn makes it a regular measure field. As a consequence, we derive several significant properties, including the measurability of the set of regular corugates and the measurability of the set of values assumed by these mappings.

The potential of high-pressure hydrogen gas mixtures with helium and oxygen as a fuel source for future power generation and transportation systems has been investigated. Using an above-threshold laser pulse, ignition was induced in hydrogen gas mixtures at pressures ranging from 10 to 100 bar and with varying levels of oxygen addition. Analysis of the resulting flames revealed that helium, despite its low reactivity, played a significant role in promoting efficient combustion. This was attributed to its ability to suppress the formation of hot gas channels that can cause combustion to fail. Additionally, the study found that the presence of helium, when combined with sufficient oxygen, allowed for stable flame propagation at relatively low pressures and at a constant velocity. This research provides new insights into the role of inert diluents in facilitating the ignition and propagation of high-pressure hydrogen flames.

Deep learning-based image segmentation has become increasingly popular in mobile and web applications. Traditional methods often rely on post-processing to enhance segmentation accuracy, particularly at object boundaries. This limitation becomes more apparent when processing images with complex edges or fine details. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel boundary-aware segmentation network (BNet). The proposed BNet integrates boundary information into both the encoder and decoder for enhanced segmentation performance. Specifically, the BNet uses a dynamic module to dynamically adjust the feature embeddings and an attention module to refine the features and predict boundaries. The proposed BNet is evaluated on multiple datasets and compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving superior results. Moreover, this BNet is designed to be efficient for deployment in mobile web applications, requiring minimal computational resources and power to deliver accurate image segmentation.

This research proposes an integrated system for enhanced driver assistance, known as lane change assistance, which relies on driver input and exchange of information between vehicles. Existing vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication technologies are employed to enable vehicles to send and receive necessary data, particularly in this application. A core component of the system is the vehicle-to-messenger (V2M) approach, which facilitates the driver's intended lane change message, transmitted to nearby vehicles via communication vehicles. A study was conducted to examine the system's effectiveness and the terms used by drivers when describing their intended actions using the V2M method.

We examine how boundaries affect a non-interacting group of weakly self-motivating particles in diverse configurations by modeling them as a modified version of the Langevin equation. The modified potential accounts for repulsion between the particles and their container as well as any external forces. The study focuses on the equilibrium characteristics of the particle distribution within the container under various external influences. To derive these properties, we establish the stationary probability distribution of the particles and calculate the mean values of their positions. The mean positions of the particles under different external influences and container shapes are calculated analytically. The findings are further verified using numerical simulations.

The average atom model is a method used to analyze the thermodynamic characteristics of materials in a radioactive environment. It has been utilized in various contexts, such as studying the properties of liquid actinides and dense plasmas. In this paper, the application of the average atom model is expanded to include the equilibrium properties of plasmas containing highly charged ions. By employing a self-consistent mean field model, it is demonstrated that including Siegert states, which describe the precise energy levels of highly charged ions, can significantly impact the chemical properties of the plasma. It is shown that accounting for the spatial characteristics of the ion's charge distribution can lead to notable differences in the plasma's thermodynamic properties.

Observations of the Si IV 1390-6 Angstrom line in a solar flare were made using the International
Radar Observatory for Astrophysics in Space (IRIS) high-resolution spectrometer (HRS) at extremely high cadences of 0.9 seconds, revealing rapid changes in the flare. The high cadence captures the initial flare peak and subsequent energy release, which caused a significant increase in the Si IV line's intensity, width, and redshift. The line profiles changed rapidly, first expanding and then contracting, which was accompanied by an increase in the line width and a gradual redshift. The initial flare peak was followed by a prolonged period of prolonged coronal heating, characterized by a decrease in the line width and a steady redshift. The high cadence observations also detected rapid changes in the flare's spatial distribution, which included a delay in the appearance of the line profiles and a subsequent southward expansion. The observed spatial distribution is consistent with the expected behavior of the coronal plasma during a flare-driven shock. The rapid changes in the flare's intensity, line profiles, and spatial distribution can be attributed to the impact of a flare-driven shock wave on the coronal plasma.

The Peccei-Quinn mechanism's original interpretation has been proven incorrect due to its failure to account for the axion's interactions with fermions. As a result, the strong CP phase cannot be explained by the axion, and a quantifiable limit exists due to the axion's role in quantum gravity. The false vacuum in the potential could cause the axion to become trapped, leading to a first-order transition and making the strong CP phase irrelevant. The initial approach to solving the strong CP problem relies on a misinterpretation of the P-Q symmetry, which is actually a false vacuum. However, even if a correct vacuum were chosen, the P-Q symmetry would still be compromised by fermions, resulting in its breakdown. To resolve this issue, a new framework is required that can naturally incorporate the P-Q symmetry, which is then broken. The breaking of this symmetry can be achieved through the interaction of a new particle, the Majoron, with the axion, leading to a solution for both the strong CP problem and the axion electric dipole moment.

A detailed examination of the impact of irradiation-induced nanopatterns in thin films through small-angle x-ray scattering (SAXS) was conducted, focusing on the influence of two key factors: the physical characteristics of thin films and the properties of radiation used. The theoretical framework of the mechanism driving this phenomenon was established in a preceding study, which explored the relationship between thin film properties and the resulting nanopattern formation, specifically the critical angle. This paper delves into the effects of radiation properties on the production of nanopatterns, with a focus on the role of the neutron form factor and the energy of radiation used. Theoretical models were developed to explain the relationship between radiation properties and the resulting nanopatterns, as well as the structural changes in films subjected to repeated radiation cycles. The theoretical predictions were found to be in agreement with experimental data, which were obtained through small-angle x-ray scattering (SAXS) experiments conducted on the experimental data collected at the National Institute of Standards and Technology's High Flux Isotope Reactor.

In software engineering, the issue of source code plagiarism is a significant challenge. A technique to identify similar programs can help address this problem. This study focuses on the applicability of routing vectors, recently introduced as a novel approach, to the software engineering field. By developing a routing vector-based framework, researchers can compare source code without requiring prior training or building a library with sample codes. A key aspect of the framework is that it allows for calculating similarity scores from any two programs. The approach is independent of language, making it suitable for programs written in languages that don't support direct program comparison. Although the approach has been demonstrated in other fields, such as network location analysis, the researchers chose to apply it to software engineering because of its unique characteristics, including the ability to differentiate between similar programs and those with distinct semantics. A key feature of the framework is its ability to calculate similarity scores. A case study was conducted to evaluate the routing approach in software engineering, specifically for programs written in C#. The results showed that the approach is feasible and can be applied to software engineering, although further investigation is required to improve its effectiveness.

We consider the Dirichlet series $F(s)$ associated with a automorphic form $f$ on a reductive group $G$ over a number field $K$. Given that $F(s)$ is absolutely convergent at $\sigma$ with a non-zero value, we can identify a novel set of points in the Bruhat-Tits building of $G$ over $K$ where the $L$-function of $F(s)$ exhibits absolute convergence.

We define approximate, metric, and norm-subgroups in metric groups and establish a representation for approximate subgroups. Our key finding demonstrates that any approximate subgroup adheres to the properties of a metric subgroup. Specifically, for groups with the left-invariant uniform structure induced from a Banach space, we identify and categorize approximate subgroups with the property of being norm-subgroups.

We introduce a novel approach to estimating densities from samples that are log-concave. This density estimation problem is significant in statistics and machine learning, particularly when working with highly structured data such as traffic flow or the movement of a robot. Our proposed density estimation method employs a Riemannian metric that is specifically defined using the probability density function itself, thereby ensuring that the resulting estimates are both smooth and concave. Our innovative density estimation method is formulated as a minimization problem and is solved using an ADMM algorithm. This density estimation method is highly versatile and can be applied to various log-concave densities in the real line, including the standard normal distribution. Our experiments show that the estimated probability density functions are visually appealing and the estimation errors are comparable to state-of-the-art methods. Our proposed density estimation method is also highly efficient and can handle large datasets from various real-world applications such as finance and social networks.

To efficiently analyze and understand the structure of granular systems, it is essential to have a reliable method for comparing and contrasting different states. The Wang-Landau algorithm is an efficient Monte Carlo technique that can be utilized to identify the most probable arrangement of particles within a given volume. By treating granular systems as isotropic and homogeneous, the method can efficiently identify the distribution of arches supporting the particles. The algorithm's results reveal that the energy landscape of granular systems is composed of a mixture of stable and metastable states with varying energies. The metastable states typically have lower energies than stable states close to the surface, while the lowest energy states are often deeply buried and may be inaccessible. The algorithm's ability to sample the various states in a granular packing enables the identification of the most probable arrangement of particles within a given volume.

The explorer and the director play a hidden strategy game on a graph with the explorer's goal of discovering every vertex first. This is achieved by the explorer moving along the edges of the graph while the director decides which vertices to color, aiming not to leave any vertex unseen. We have analyzed this explorer-director game on complete bipartite graphs and obtained specific results for a particular case. Moreover, a comparison is made between the explorer-director model and traditional pursuit and evasion games on complete bipartite graphs.

We examine how frequencies vary over time in the spectrum of a specific type of random process, focusing on the fluctuations that occur randomly. We find that the relationship between consecutive frequencies depends on the specific characteristics of the process, such as its variance, mean, and the rate at which frequencies change over time. This relationship can be either positive, negative, or zero, and it's determined by how quickly the process's mean frequency changes, as well as by the type of correlation within the process. In cases where there's no correlation within the process, the relationship between consecutive frequencies is directly proportional to the rate at which frequencies change, but is affected by how quickly the process's mean frequency changes. However, in cases where there's strong correlation within the process, the relationship can be both positive and negative, and it's dependent on the properties of the process's variance.

In this paper, the one-dimensional higher-order Broer-Kaup system is analyzed and two types of interaction solutions are proposed: Riemann function solutions and superposition solutions. The solutions are derived from a constant matrix T and two specific constant vectors p and q. The resulting interaction solutions are then tested with initial conditions and their characteristics are examined.

Inspired by the work of Chen-Gang in [12], this study confirms that in an arbitrary dimension, (1) the Cauchy problem for 3D incompressible Euler equations, under certain initial and boundary conditions, has a conserved energy solution when the initial vorticity falls within a particular class of functions. The approach relies on an enhanced version of the div-curl inequality and the concept of weak solutions as introduced by R. Temam.

The VIRUP project offers a set of tools for immersive virtual reality experiences, allowing users to explore and interact with a vast, photorealistic universe simulation based on Lambdas-Standard Model cosmology. The universe simulation is powered by a mesh-based code, Enzo, and features intricate galaxy structures, filaments, and galaxy spectra generated through complex astrophysical simulations. A custom application, designed to run on VR headsets, enables users to navigate and engage with the digital universe through a range of interactive tools, including a spatial locator, visualizer, and query-based interface. The toolset is flexible, with the ability to be adapted to various simulations and user groups, and is being made available to the community under an open-source license.

The Data Bricks Space Mission is a hands-on learning activity grounded in data
physicalization, developed to help kids aged 10-12 understand data principles.
Drawing on research from the Data Structures in the Age of Big Data Study,
this intervention was designed to explore how data structure learning compares
when using real-world versus simulated data. Through a mixed-methods approach,
we conducted a pilot and discovered that the Data Bricks Space Mission is an
effective means of teaching data structures, and our findings also shed light
on the benefits and limitations of data structure learning via physicalized data.
Our results show that using real data offers advantages, such as increased
relevance and authenticity, but poses challenges like increased complexity.
Moreover, physicalized data provides a more engaging learning experience and
fosters deeper understanding among students.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to discovering data-path details in software-defined networks using deep-packet inspection technology. The proposed method involves constructing a comprehensive set of possible data-path configurations, refining this list through structural analysis, and testing each potential configuration by sending a minimal set of packets. The non-matching configurations are eliminated in successive iterations, allowing for real-time discovery of data-path details in real-time environments. The proposed method's efficiency is demonstrated through experiments in real-time environments and comparisons with existing state-of-the-art techniques, which show its superiority in achieving accurate results with significantly reduced packet transmission requirements.

Recent advancements in weak supervision have led to the development of a new class of unsupervised and semi-supervised learning techniques. These methods utilize diverse forms of data like images, text, videos, and graphs to capture multiple viewpoints of the data. However, the inherent relational information within graph-structured data is often underutilized. Our research demonstrates that incorporating relational information enhances the performance of weakly supervised learning models, yielding improved results in tasks like visual classification and prediction. We introduce a novel framework, the Weakly Disentangled Representation Graph Network, which combines self-supervised training with graph attention mechanisms to capture multiple viewpoints of data and capture strong class relationships. Our experiments on image classification, text-based image retrieval, video recognition, and graph classification tasks showcase the efficacy of our approach.

The concept of tidal and wave energy harvesting through the manipulation of the complex interactions between the wake and multiple oscillating foils is explored in this study. The wake's behavior, particularly in relation to its shape and shedding, is investigated for various foil configurations, including both low and high Reynolds number conditions. The dependence of the wake's characteristics on the ratio of Strouhal number to slip speed, as well as the distance between the foils and the mean flow speed, is examined. Theoretical and experimental models are used to understand the physical mechanisms behind the wake's behavior, and the efficiency of energy harvesting is estimated for various foil configurations, including equal spacing and tandem arrangements. The findings suggest that optimal energy harvesting occurs when the wake is shed at a high Strouhal number, and the results are compared with existing literature. The study also explores the feasibility of using multiple foils in a row, and the results are extended to include the effects of foil aspect ratio and wake blockage.

We've developed a dynamic Bayesian inference framework, utilizing a Gaussian mixture model, to continuously update and refine the results for real-time observables in non-relativistic QCD calculations. This approach enables the determination of statistical and systematic uncertainties throughout the real-time spectrum, facilitating an objective evaluation of the model's parameters. Applying our framework to the lattice QCD computation of the heavy quark free energy, we've obtained more accurate results, particularly in regions with substantial uncertainties in traditional methods. Furthermore, our method allows the dynamic evolution of uncertainties throughout the real-time domain, providing valuable insights into the underlying physical processes.

Our team has developed a method to observe the interaction between a quantum dot and a superconducting island through electrical means, allowing for the detection of individual charge-tunneling events. This is made possible by converting the control voltage applied to the quantum dot into a measurable current, enabling us to identify single Cooper pairs either being tunneled or reflected. By analyzing the current in real time, we were able to measure the probability distribution of the quantum dot's charge state and found it follows a pattern characteristic of an Arrhenius distribution. Furthermore, we found that this behavior is consistent even when the quantum dot is coupled with multiple superconducting islands, and the current-voltage relationship remains coherent. This gate sensing technique offers new possibilities for studying quantum systems and quantum dot-based sensors.

The primary goal in drug discovery processes is to identify potential candidate drugs with specific therapeutic effects. By employing a generative model, it's possible to create new compounds with desired properties, which are often represented as subgraphs within molecular graphs. In this study, we introduce the SMILE-GEM approach, which integrates a data-driven energy-based generative model for learning flexible distributions of molecular graphs from SMILE code. Our model generates candidate compounds with improved efficacy and reduced side effects for specific targets. Our experiments demonstrate that SMILE-GEM surpasses current methods by a considerable margin, as measured by the average log-probability of targeted drugs. Additionally, we find that our generated compounds exhibit enhanced target-specific activity and a significantly lower incidence of adverse side effects.

The Graph Path Reconfiguration Algorithm (GPRA) is a powerful tool for transforming graphs according to specific rules, ensuring that each step adheres to a set of constraints. By applying this algorithm, we can create an efficient and space-efficient computation model that is comparable to the Dynamic GoI machine. This model, which is based on GPRA, can represent lambda-graphical logic and has the potential to become a more efficient version of lambda calculus by utilizing a graph structure to replace the environment in lambda graphs. Furthermore, this graph calculus can be implemented in a space-efficient manner with a near-linear time complexity, making it a promising candidate for large-scale computation.

We've conducted an in-depth analysis of the LMC's outer regions, incorporating data from the second VLBI survey of the Large Magellanic Cloud, along with the Victoria Street Array's latest observations. By combining these findings with data from the 2MASS and VMC surveys, we've identified 1.8 x 10^4 stars within a 3 x 5 degree grid. By applying a matching algorithm to the stars in the grid, we've established a reference frame for the LMC, enabling us to determine the stars' motion relative to the LMC center. Our research has revealed that the stars within this area exhibit a range of motion patterns, from circular motions to outward trajectories. Notably, we've identified a distinct group of high-velocity stars moving away from the LMC, which we propose may be stars being pulled away by the Small Magellanic Cloud. Our analysis also suggests that the stars within this area exhibit a higher level of proper motion noise than the overall LMC.

Deep learning models can accurately identify electricity theft in smart grids by analyzing energy usage patterns over time. Nonetheless, the numerous variables that govern model performance pose a significant challenge to achieving optimal results. This study presents a novel, automated approach to fine-tune deep learning models capable of detecting electricity theft that adapts to the specific configuration of its hyper-parameters through recurrent neural networks combined with genetic algorithms. The proposed method does not necessitate the manual adjustment of hyper-parameters and can adapt to different energy systems. The results of this study demonstrate that the new approach surpasses conventional techniques in detecting electricity theft and suggests that the genetic algorithm used is robust to different smart grid datasets. The method exhibits high accuracy in detecting electricity theft while minimizing false positives and minimizing the impact of false negatives on energy usage forecasting.

We propose a new method for creating tight surface graphs inductively using specific graph properties. The primary goal is to develop all tight surface graphs within a particular class of graphs by gradually adding new vertices and connections between existing ones. The introduced technique can be applied to the following types of surface graphs: those on a specific surface with a particular surface code, surface graphs embedded in a 2-dimensional space, surface graphs defined on a particular type of spherical graph, surface graphs defined on a torus or doughnut shape, surface graphs defined on a sphere or other spherical surfaces, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable sphere or surface, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable projective plane, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable sphere, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable elliptic surface, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable torus, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable projective sphere, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable projective sphere with a particular type of surface code, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable projective sphere with a different type of surface code, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable elliptical sphere, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable elliptical torus, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable projective sphere with a different type of surface code, surface graphs defined on a non-orientable projective sphere with a different type of surface code, surface graphs defined on

The lifetimes of $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons have been measured through a precise timing analysis conducted by the LHCb experiment using data collected from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 2 inverse femtobarns. The results show that the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ lifetimes are 436.2 $\pm 3.2$ $\mu$s and 186.4 $\pm 2.5$ $\mu$s respectively, both significantly shorter than the world average and standard value for the $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ lifetime. The results contradict the current understanding of cusp-like behavior in the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and provide the most accurate measurements to date of $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ lifetime.

Hyperspectral image classification is a critical task in remote sensing with various applications. The classification of such images has been significantly improved through the integration of spectral-spatial patterns, however, existing methods often struggle with noisy data and lack the ability to capture the complex relationships within spectral-spatial data. To address these limitations, a novel approach called Fast and Accurate Similarity-constrained Subspace Clustering (FAS2) has been developed, combining the strengths of local similarity constraint and spectral-spatial relationships. The proposed method consists of two main stages: the first stage involves constructing a local similarity graph and identifying the most significant nodes for each class, while the second stage leverages these similarities to estimate the final class labels. The effectiveness of FAS2 has been validated through experiments on three hyperspectral datasets, where it significantly outperformed 24 state-of-the-art methods and achieved impressive accuracy with a computational cost that is only one-fifth to one-tenth of other top performers.

Arctic sea ice's surface features small snow undulations, dubbed "snow dunes", which arise from the weight of snow on flat ice.  These features are crucial for understanding ice-atomizer performance, snow accumulation, and ice thickness in the Arctic.  However, the exact mechanisms behind their formation are still unknown.  To address this, researchers developed an idealized model that simulates the characteristics of these snow dunes.  By analyzing the model's outcomes, the team discovered that the model accurately replicates the scale and spatial patterns of real-world snow dunes on undeformed ice.  These findings suggest that the model can predict the spatial and temporal patterns of real-world snow dunes, and can be used to investigate the underlying dynamics of these features.

Our study explores the quantum Zeno effect in ultracold atom-molecule collisions,
utilizing high-frequency magnetic fields with low amplitude variations. 
The average outcome of these collisions can be significantly altered by
temporarily blocking transitions between specific energy states, often resulting
in increased reaction rates. This phenomenon is notably observed in cases where
the initial atomic state has a high angular momentum, contrary to conventional
expectations which suggest that such interactions should be suppressed. 
The effectiveness of the quantum Zeno effect in these situations, however, hinges
on the specific energy levels involved and the corresponding coupling strengths.

We investigate the impact of non-extensive statistical properties on stochastic processes within the It\^o-Langevin framework, yielding novel equations that extend the standard Langevin equation through a q-deformed transport coefficient and modified dissipation term. These modified dynamics are examined in the context of a particle's random energy fluctuations within a thermal bath, resulting in a q-deformed central momentum spectrum that deviates from the Gaussian distribution, even as the system approaches equilibrium.

The emergence of nonrelativistic topology, characterized by the Weyl node, is typically triggered by magnetic fields. However, our research reveals that finite intensity of a propagating light wave can also cause the formation of Weyl nodes within a semimetal known as nodal-line band. The findings demonstrate that the optical field significantly accelerates the formation of Weyl nodes at a much quicker rate than temperature-based methods. The discovery also shows that the optical field induces a unique type of topological structure known as the topological charge, which is not achievable through temperature-based methods. The study's outcomes provide new insights into the potential uses of light in manipulating and engineering topological materials, which could lead to innovative photonic devices and technologies.

This paper introduces a new decentralized computing protocol, Marvel DC, that enables a decentralized computational task market. We establish a security model and a formal model for decentralized computing tasks, and develop a secure protocol, decentralized computing contracts, to facilitate the exchange of computation resources. We extend this protocol to a blockchain environment, incorporating incentives, to create Marvel DC. Empirical results indicate that Marvel DC is both secure and resistant to incentive manipulation, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed solution.

A new metric is proposed for assessing the quality of 3D point cloud compression, 
which can be accurately predicted using a machine learning model.  The learning 
model was trained with data from a large, point cloud quality reduction dataset,
